topic: Sentence Rearrangement PQRS (Verbal Ability and Reading Comprehension)

sections.title: Basic Concept of Sentence Rearrangement PQRS
sections.content: In Sentence Rearrangement, a sentence is divided into four parts: P, Q, R, and S. These parts must be arranged in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence. In this type of question, identifying the subject, verb, object, and the logical flow of the sentence is important.

sections.title: Identifying Subject–Verb–Object
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the part that contains the subject (such as he, she, Ram, the king). Step 2: The verb part usually follows (such as went, built, saw). Step 3: Finally, the object or additional information appears. Example: Ram → built → a small house.

sections.title: Prepositional Phrase Connection
sections.content: Step 1: Identify prepositions such as in, on, at, near, under. Step 2: These usually connect with a noun or place. Step 3: Place them after the word they relate to. Example: 'in the garden' usually comes after the noun it describes.

sections.title: Basic Conjunction Clues
sections.content: Step 1: Identify conjunctions such as and, but, because. Step 2: These words connect two ideas. Step 3: Usually the main idea appears first and the conjunction clause follows. Example: 'He was tired because he worked all day.'

sections.title: Daily Event Based Sentences
sections.content: At Level 1, sentences are usually based on everyday events, simple facts, or small stories. Therefore, understanding the meaning of the sentence and recognizing the natural order of events is important.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Starting the sentence with a verb. 2. Placing a prepositional phrase in the wrong position. 3. Beginning the sentence with a conjunction unnecessarily. 4. Arranging the sentence using only grammar without understanding the meaning.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: In PQRS rearrangement, first identify the subject, then arrange the verb and object logically. Prepositional phrases and conjunctions should be connected according to the meaning of the sentence.

tricks.title: Subject First Rule
tricks.explanation: Most sentences usually begin with the subject.

tricks.title: Verb Placement Trick
tricks.explanation: The verb usually comes after the subject.

tricks.title: Preposition Attachment Trick
tricks.explanation: A prepositional phrase usually comes after the noun it modifies.
tricks.example: The book on the table is mine.

tricks.title: Conjunction Linking Trick
tricks.explanation: Words like and, but, because connect two ideas.
tricks.example: He was late because the bus broke down.

tricks.title: Meaning Flow Trick
tricks.explanation: Read the sentence to check whether the order of events sounds natural.
tricks.example: He woke up early and went for a walk.

tricks.title: Ending Phrase Check
tricks.explanation: Information about place or time often appears at the end of a sentence.

tricks.title: Pronoun Reference Trick
tricks.explanation: A pronoun should come after the noun it refers to.
tricks.example: Ravi bought a car and he was very happy.

tricks.title: Quick Pair Method
tricks.explanation: First identify two parts that are clearly connected.
tricks.example: A clause containing 'because' usually connects with a reason.
